articles.title: A Utah couple began cycling across America on their 40th wedding anniversary; 87 days and 3,634 miles later, they reached the Atlantic coast and raised about $23,000 for two community charities
articles.summary: A Utah couple celebrated four decades of marriage by cycling across the United States, completing an 87-day journey from Washington to New Jersey and
articles.body: A Utah couple celebrated four decades of marriage by cycling across the United States, completing an 87-day journey from Washington to New Jersey and raising approximately $23,000 for two community charities. According to Deseret News, Robert and Bliss Sawyer finished their coast-to-coast adventure in September 2026, turning a personal milestone into a fundraising effort for affordable housing and food assistance. Their journey, documented on their website, Hope Across the USA, was also covered by Utah broadcaster KSL ahead of their departure.The couple began their ride on June 20, their 40th wedding anniversary, in Bellingham, Washington, where they first met. Nearly three months later, on September 12, they reached Ocean City, New Jersey, bringing their long-distance cycling challenge to an end at the Atlantic coast. By then, they had covered 3,634 miles and climbed more than 96,000 feet in elevation, navigating mountain passes, changing weather and long stretches of unfamiliar roads.A journey driven by purposeThe Sawyers, who live in Saratoga Springs, Utah, named their initiative Hope Across the USA. Their goal was to combine an ambitious cycling challenge with support for two causes they care about: Habitat for Humanity and Tabitha’s Way Local Food Pantry.Bliss Sawyer, 59, works as a mortgage loan officer and wanted to support efforts to improve access to stable housing. Her husband, Robert, 64, is a retired exercise physiology professor who has volunteered with Tabitha’s Way, a Utah-based organisation that helps people facing food insecurity. The couple raised around $23,000 during the trip, using their journey to draw attention to the needs of families who struggle to secure housing and put food on the table.From the Pacific to the AtlanticThe route took the cyclists across the northern United States, beginning in Washington and passing through Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan. They then travelled through Indiana, Ohio and Pennsylvania before reaching the New Jersey coast. The couple averaged about 48 miles a day, although their daily distances varied considerably. Their longest ride covered nearly 70 miles, while their shortest was about 20 miles.Their accommodation changed with the terrain and circumstances. They spent 34 nights camping, booked 27 nights in hotels and stayed 26 nights with hosts who offered free accommodation through Warmshowers, a hospitality network for touring cyclists. Despite the physical demands, the journey offered opportunities to experience the country at a slower pace. The Sawyers passed through mountain landscapes, open farmland, forests and lakeside routes, while also encountering communities and people they might otherwise have missed travelling by car.Learning to ride togetherThe cross-country challenge built on decades of cycling together. The couple began riding regularly around 2000, gradually progressing from shorter outings to longer cycling holidays in the United States and abroad. Previous adventures included rides across parts of Britain and a six-week cycling trip through Norway.Their latest journey, however, demanded sustained effort over nearly three months. Heat, rain, mechanical problems and difficult climbs tested their endurance, while spending almost every day together required patience and communication.One particularly difficult stretch came after a navigation mistake led them onto a steep, rocky trail where they had to push their bicycles. Frustration and misunderstandings followed, but the couple eventually stopped to talk through what had happened. The experience reinforced the importance of recognising each other’s intentions rather than assuming the worst, a lesson that helped them approach the remainder of the trip with greater understanding.For the Sawyers, reaching the Atlantic was more than the completion of a physical challenge. It marked the end of a journey built around a shared interest, a significant anniversary and a commitment to helping others. Their ride demonstrated how a personal milestone can become an opportunity to support community causes, with thousands of miles on the road translating into financial assistance for people in need.You use AI every day. articles.title: Strong pushback as US downgrades Hong Kong to tier-3 in human trafficking: 'Double standard'
articles.summary: Hong Kong has rejected the United States’ decision to place it in the lowest category of its annual human trafficking report, calling the assessment
articles.body: Hong Kong has rejected the United States’ decision to place it in the lowest category of its annual human trafficking report, calling the assessment “entirely unfounded” and accusing Washington of applying double standards in evaluating the city’s efforts to combat trafficking. The US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report, released on October 8, downgraded Hong Kong to Tier 3 from the Tier 2 Watch List, where it had remained for two consecutive years. The lowest tier includes mainland China, Macau, North Korea, Russia, Iran and Afghanistan.In a statement, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government strongly rejected the assessment, describing it as an attempt to damage the city’s reputation. It maintained that human trafficking had never been prevalent in Hong Kong and disputed the US assertion that the city was not making significant efforts to eliminate the crime.The US report, however, said Hong Kong did not fully meet the minimum standards for eliminating trafficking and had fallen short in prosecuting suspected traffickers and identifying victims exploited within the territory.The tier rankings assess governments’ efforts to combat human trafficking, rather than the prevalence of trafficking itself.What the US report said about Hong KongAccording to the report, Hong Kong authorities investigated 11 human trafficking cases in 2025, all involving forced labour, compared with seven cases in 2024. However, authorities prosecuted one suspect, down from two the previous year, while two sex traffickers were convicted. One of those convicted received a prison sentence of less than a year.The report also raised concerns about victim identification. Despite conducting approximately 12,100 initial screenings in 2025, authorities identified no victims who had been exploited within Hong Kong.All 15 victims identified during the year were Hong Kong residents who had fallen prey to employment fraud and been forced to work in scam centres in Myanmar and Cambodia, the report said.The Hong Kong government confirmed the screening and victim figures but said the number of screenings had increased by 7 per cent from the previous year. It argued that bringing residents home safely, identifying them as trafficking victims and investigating those implicated demonstrated its commitment to tackling the crime.A government spokesman accused the US of hypocrisy, citing studies and reports that had highlighted the underreporting of human trafficking cases by American law enforcement agencies.The US report reiterated its criticism that Hong Kong lacks a single law criminalising all forms of human trafficking. Instead, authorities rely on a range of offences relating to prostitution, immigration, employment and physical abuse.The Hong Kong government defended its legal framework, saying more than 50 legal provisions address trafficking-related conduct and provide safeguards comparable to those available under dedicated anti-trafficking legislation in other jurisdictions.“There is simply no one-size-fits-all solution,” the government spokesman said.The report criticized Hong Kong’s rules governing foreign domestic workers, particularly the live-in requirement and the “two-week rule”, which generally requires workers whose employment ends to leave Hong Kong within two weeks unless they obtain permission to remain.According to the US assessment, these arrangements could increase workers’ vulnerability to exploitation by employers and employment agencies. It also raised concerns that agencies routinely charged fees exceeding the legal limit and that penalties were insufficient to deter violations.Hong Kong has approximately 380,000 foreign domestic workers.Defending the arrangements, the Hong Kong government said the live-in requirement supported its policy of giving local workers priority in employment. It added that domestic workers who experienced abuse or exploitation could apply to change employers without first returning to their home countries.The government said employment agencies could charge workers no more than 10 per cent of their first month’s salary following successful placement. It also cited more than 1,700 inspections of domestic worker employment agencies in 2025 and the arrest of 37 employers in connection with physical or sexual abuse of domestic workers.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oxford ceremony marks return home of kiwi feather cloak
articles.summary: The kahu kiwi, given to a British doctor in 1900, was "crying to come home", Māori campaigners say.
articles.body:
A ceremony has been held to mark the return of a Māori kiwi feather cloak to New Zealand by a British museum.

The kahu kiwi was one of the farewell gifts presented by Māori leaders in 1900 to Dr George Cleghorn, a medical doctor who had been working in New Zealand.

It was loaned to the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford by Cleghorn's widow in 1913.

The Homebound Project, a charity which funded the return, said the cloak was "crying to come home".

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

Dr Lorraine Eade, chair of Ngāti Rārua o Te Wairau Society, which now owns the item, said its significance was "beyond measure".

She said its return was an opportunity to acknowledge Cleghorn's work for Māori people.

The doctor advocated for their right to attend a local hospital instead of being required to travel further afield for medical treatment, Pitt Rivers Museum said.

He also spent time educating families at their homes on the importance of taking public health measures, it added.

Shane Graham, chief executive of Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Rārua, a Māori authority, said the return was a momentous occasion.

"It restores mana [prestige] and honours the deep emotional and cultural significance of our living connection to this taonga [treasure]," he said.

Prof Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum, said: "We are very pleased that the day has come for the Kahu Kiwi to return home."

A ceremony was held in Oxford earlier to mark the cloak's departure.

articles.title: After a New York fire killed a 13-year-old girl's father and four sisters, relatives raised over $100,000 for her; months later, the state AG sought $71,539.29 it said remained unpaid
articles.summary: A New York teenager who lost her father and four sisters in a devastating house fire was at the centre of a legal dispute months later, after relatives
articles.body: A New York teenager who lost her father and four sisters in a devastating house fire was at the centre of a legal dispute months later, after relatives who raised more than $100,000 to support her allegedly failed to hand over most of the money. According to a 2019 report by WWNY-TV and court documents cited by the broadcaster, the New York Attorney General’s office sought the return of $71,539.29, alleging that the funds had been improperly spent and that investigators had been misled about the money. The case was filed in New York State Supreme Court in October 2019 by then-Attorney General Letitia James. The state alleged that the relatives had not transferred the full amount to Hailey or her mother, Melissa Davey, despite repeated requests for an accounting. The original court petition also alleged that the fundraisers had failed to comply with state requirements governing charitable donations. WWNY-TV⁠ and the court petition⁠ detailed the allegations.A community came together after the tragedyThe fire broke out on February 14, 2019, at the family’s home on Myrtle Avenue in Watertown, New York. Hailey’s father, Aaron Bodah, and her four sisters, Merissa, Alexa, Erin and Skylar, died in the blaze. Hailey, then 13, was the only surviving child in the family.The tragedy prompted an outpouring of support from the local community. A GoFundMe campaign organised on behalf of Kenneth Bodah raised $25,680 through 523 donations, according to the fundraising page⁠ . Other efforts included community fundraisers and donations collected through a memorial fund and a union-related initiative.The fundraising was intended to help Hailey following the loss of her immediate family. In a letter published in the local newspaper, her paternal relatives had reportedly assured donors that the money would be managed responsibly and used for her benefit, according to the state’s court filing.How the donations came under scrutinyThe Attorney General’s office began seeking financial records after learning that the funds had not been transferred to Hailey or her mother within the period specified under state law. According to the petition, the relatives were asked in August 2019 to disclose the total amount raised, identify where the money was being held and explain how the funds would be handed over. A cashier’s cheque for $35,021.61 was delivered to Hailey on September 20, 2019, through the relatives’ lawyer.However, investigators subsequently obtained bank records that showed $97,199.29 had been deposited into an account called the Bodah Family Memorial Fund between February 19 and September 23, 2019. The state alleged that a substantial portion of the money remained unaccounted for or had been spent on purchases that were not consistent with the stated purpose of the fundraising.The records cited in the petition included more than $5,300 in purchases from Lowe’s, a home improvement retailer, covering household appliances and other supplies. A further $453.86 was spent at an online home furnishings retailer, according to the filing. The state also identified payments to a church and a monument company. It argued that the donations had been solicited specifically for Hailey and that the money should not have been diverted to other expenses without the appropriate basis.State sought the return of more than $71,000By October 2019, the Attorney General’s office was seeking the transfer of the remaining $71,539.29 to Hailey, through her mother and legal guardian. It also requested penalties and a full accounting of the money raised through the different fundraising efforts.Kenneth Bodah Jr., Beth Ann Bodah and Travis Bodah were accused of failing to turn over the donations as required by law. The petition further accused Kenneth and Beth of making false statements to investigators, while Kenneth was separately accused of fraud.These were allegations contained in the state’s legal filing, rather than findings of guilt. WWNY-TV reported at the time that it had been unable to reach the three relatives for comment. The case highlighted the questions that can arise when donations are collected for a named individual after a tragedy, particularly when relatives or other organisers control the funds before they reach the intended beneficiary. In Hailey’s case, the state sought to ensure that the money raised in the aftermath of an unimaginable loss was delivered to the teenager it was meant to support.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bangor worker paralysed after falling 30ft wins £10m from employer
articles.summary: The HSE found Gavin Pugh's injuries could have been prevented if correct safety steps were followed.
articles.body:
A maintenance worker whose life was "turned upside down" when he fell 30ft from a power line and was left paralysed has won at least £10m in compensation.

Gavin Pugh was dismantling a pylon in April 2022 when he unknowingly clipped his safety line to a section that was only secure at one end.

His safety rope slipped loose, causing him to plunge to the ground and suffer life-changing injuries to his brain, neck, shoulder, ribs and internal organs which mean he needs a wheelchair for the rest of his life.

Pugh, who was 33 at the time, sued his employer, Wood Transmission and Distribution Ltd, after the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found "adequate safety arrangements" had not been in place.

The Cheshire-based firm was fined £240,000 at a magistrates' court hearing in 2024 over the HSE's findings, before facing High Court proceedings brought by Pugh, from Bangor, Gwynedd.

HSE inspector Robert Gidman told the court the "tragic incident" could have been prevented if the company had "adequate arrangements to protect its workers from harm".

The pylon in Staffordshire had already been worked on by others, with a nut left loose, but this was not something Pugh knew about.

"Proper assessment of the risks and consideration of work methods, adequate staffing and clear procedures for transferring towers between teams could have enabled this work to go ahead without incident," Gidman added.

"Instead, because of the company's shortcomings, a worker has sadly and unnecessarily been left paralysed."

After out-of-court negotiations, a care and compensation package was agreed, described by Pugh's lawyers as worth "eight figures".

The money was compensation for his injuries and lost future earnings, as well as to help fund 24-hour live-in carers and more than £1m in rehabilitation costs.

Pugh's lawyers said that, before the fall, he had been an "active and sociable person" who enjoyed his job and had his own fishing boat.

But his injuries left him unable to walk and suffering "life-changing physical limitations" and "significant psychological consequences".

The firm, Stewarts, secured interim payments to fund his vital private rehab and care while negotiations were taking place.

Pugh said the incident "turned my life upside down".

"I wasn't able to work or go out with my friends. My life fell apart," he said.

He added that he was "very grateful" for the settlement, which would allow him to regain some quality of life, adding he had already been able to "get back into some of my past hobbies".

"I'm fishing and I'm able to get out and about. I'm able to go out with my friends again and enjoy myself, albeit not to the same extent, but I'm still happy."

Wood Transmission and Distribution Ltd, now known as United Infrastructure Power T&D Ltd, has been asked to comment.

articles.title: Northern Lights: Aurora stun UK down to England's south coast
articles.summary: The natural phenomenon, known as the Aurora Borealis, is the result of increased solar activity.
articles.body:
Residents across the UK were left stunned as the sky was illuminated by the spectacular colours of the Northern Lights on Friday and Saturday evenings.

The natural phenomenon, known as the Aurora Borealis, is the result of increased solar activity.

Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland, but particularly strong activity levels meant they could be seen as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent on Saturday night.

The Met Office has said sightings could continue to be possible during clear skies until Tuesday.

Northern Lights are caused by powerful solar eruptions from the Sun, called coronal mass ejections (CMEs).

Towards the end of last week, the Sun was observed to unleash CMEs directed towards the Earth.

This stream of charged particles can get captured by the Earth's magnetic field and directed into our atmosphere, especially towards polar regions.

When these charged particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen, photons of coloured light are emitted - this is the aurora.

The chances of seeing the aurora vary across the UK depending upon its strength. When activity levels reach 200nT (nanotesla) the aurora would be visible in the north of the UK, but not the south.

On Saturday evening, those levels reached 600nT, meaning it would be visible across the whole of the UK, even in the south, which is a much rarer phenomenon.

Experts have previously said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting as the Sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.

If you missed out this time, the aurora may return on Sunday.

The Met Office has said sightings remain possible across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies until Tuesday.

To see them, you need to look northwards, away from bright streetlights, and look through a mobile phone camera.

The reason you need to use a camera is because in low-light conditions at night our eyes use rod cells to see - these cells do not perceive colour and so we actually see in black and white. Cameras do not have the same limitations.

articles.title: Hurricane Simon strengthens to Category 4 off Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.summary: Puerto Vallarta businesses board up windows as Hurricane Simon threatens Mexico’s west-central coast.
articles.body:
Hurricane Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast, packing winds of up to 241km/h (150mph) as it threatens to bring destructive winds, storm surges and life-threatening flooding to southwestern Mexico.

The US National Hurricane Center said that Simon was expected to approach or move just inland of Mexico’s west-central coast late on Saturday or early Sunday. The storm was about 115 miles (185km) south-southwest of Manzanillo, with further strengthening possible before landfall.

The hurricane could bring 10 to 20 inches (25 to 51cm) of rain to parts of southwestern Mexico through Sunday.

“This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the agency warned, urging residents to complete preparations to protect lives and property.

Authorities issued a hurricane warning for parts of the Pacific coast south of the resort city of Puerto Vallarta, including the area around Manzanillo, the country’s largest Pacific port. A tropical storm watch was in effect farther south towards Lazaro Cardenas.

Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas. Officials also urged hotels and other tourism businesses in Puerto Vallarta to ensure workers and visitors had access to shelters or safe locations.

Businesses in the popular tourist destination boarded up windows and placed sandbags at entrances as the storm approached.

The hurricane centre also warned of a dangerous storm surge and large and destructive waves near where Simon makes landfall.

articles.title: In 2012, Taylor Swift pledged $4 million for a Nashville education centre; 14 years later, the space is showcasing artwork by local schoolchildren and artists with developmental disabilities
articles.summary: Taylor Swift’s $4 million gift to the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum in 2012 helped create a dedicated education centre in Nashville.
articles.body: Taylor Swift’s $4 million gift to the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum in 2012 helped create a dedicated education centre in Nashville. The space was designed for more than music lessons: it would give children and families room to learn, experiment and engage with country music’s history. Fourteen years later, the centre is hosting Connection, an exhibition of posters created by Metro Nashville Public Schools students and artists from Friends Life Community, a nonprofit serving adults with developmental disabilities. The museum says the participants explored the history and techniques of Hatch Show Print, its historic letterpress shop, before making their own work. The exhibition brings the centre’s original educational promise to life, showing how a space built for learning can keep opening doors to creativity and community.A major gift for educationIn May 2012, Swift pledged $4 million towards a new education centre at the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum. According to MusicRow, it was the largest capital contribution by an individual artist in the museum’s 45-year history at the time. The museum named the centre in her honour.The gift formed part of a wider expansion campaign called 'Working on a Building: Country Music Lives Here'. The museum planned to grow from 140,000 square feet to more than 350,000 square feet, creating additional exhibition and learning spaces as well as new visitor facilities.The Taylor Swift Education Center was planned as a space of more than 7,500 square feet, spread across parts of two floors. Its design included three classrooms and a children’s exhibition gallery. The museum expected its new facilities to increase its educational capacity by as much as sevenfold.The planned classrooms were intended for a range of activities, from the museum’s flagship Words & Music programme to family events and distance learning. One “wet classroom” was designed for hands-on projects that could get messy, including letterpress art activities connected to Hatch Show Print.Learning by makingThe centre’s original vision was not limited to traditional classroom instruction. The museum planned spaces where students could explore objects, observe curators at work and take part in activities that made music history tangible. A visible storage area and design studio would allow visitors to see how museum professionals handle and interpret collections.That hands-on approach is reflected in the centre’s current exhibition, Connection. Opened in 2026, the show brings together posters made by Metro Nashville Public Schools students and artists engaged with Friends Life Community. The project began with visits to Hatch Show Print, the museum’s nearly 150-year-old letterpress shop. Students learned about the shop’s history, studied design principles and explored how letterpress printing works. They then created shapes using foam and sponges, printed those forms and used them as inspiration for their finished posters, as per reports.The process gave participants a chance to learn not only by looking at art, but by making it. They experimented with words, images, colour and composition, using the print shop’s techniques to develop their own visual ideas.Two groups, one exhibitionThe exhibition also grew from a collaboration between the museum and Friends Life Community, which serves adults with developmental disabilities. Friends Life invited Hatch Show Print Master Printer Emeritus Jim Sherraden to work as a teaching artist in residence in 2023. In late 2024, artists from Friends Life Community visited the print shop for a behind-the-presses tour. Sherraden and Jennifer Haston, the organisation’s visual arts programme coordinator, helped participants bring their words, lettering and images to life through poster-making, as per reports.The posters created by both groups form the exhibition’s central focus. The museum says the works use action words and imagery to imagine a future where people connect through creative art and social causes. The title Connection speaks to the ideas behind the exhibition, but also to the relationships built through the process: between students and artists, participants and printers, and the public and the museum.The project demonstrates how a museum education space can bring people together across ages and abilities. It also gives visitors the opportunity to encounter work made by members of their own community, rather than only by established artists or historical figures.A centre still doing its jobWhen Swift made her pledge, the museum described the centre as a place for school groups, families, young people and adults. The new exhibition shows how that original ambition continues to shape the space more than a decade later.The education centre is not simply a room named after a famous musician. It is part of the museum’s broader effort to connect people with country music and its creative traditions through participation. In Connection, that means learning about letterpress printing, trying the process and producing posters that reflect the creators’ own ideas.The exhibition is open to museum visitors, with admission included in the price of a museum ticket. The museum also offers free admission for local youth and discounted tickets for up to two accompanying adults from Davidson County and neighbouring counties, with proof of residency.From a pledge to a public platformSwift’s $4 million contribution helped establish a permanent place for education within one of Nashville’s best-known cultural institutions. The classrooms, children’s gallery and hands-on programming were designed to make the museum more than a place to view exhibits. They made room for visitors to learn through doing.Fourteen years later, the posters in Connection offer a vivid example of that idea in practice. Local students and artists with developmental disabilities have explored a historic printing tradition and used it to express their own perspectives.The exhibition does not mark the end of the centre’s story. It reflects what can happen when a cultural institution invests in space, teaching and creative access over time. A gift made in 2012 helped build the setting; the people using it today are filling that setting with their own work, ideas and connections.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Harvard bought this stained document for $27.50; decades later, experts realised it was an original Magna Carta
articles.summary: Harvard Law School bought a stained and faded parchment in 1946 for just $27.50, believing it was an ordinary later copy of the Magna Carta.
articles.body: Harvard Law School bought a stained and faded parchment in 1946 for just $27.50, believing it was an ordinary later copy of the Magna Carta. The document was catalogued as dating from 1327 and remained in the library for decades. Nearly 80 years later, medieval historians examining a digital image noticed that something about it did not fit that description. Further research and specialist imaging eventually showed that the parchment was an original version issued by King Edward I in 1300, making it one of only seven surviving copies of that edition.Harvard’s $27.50 Magna Carta remained unrecognised for decadesThe document, identified as HLS MS 172, had long been treated as an unremarkable copy. Harvard Law School’s records show that the library bought it in 1946 for $27.50 after it had been sold through a London book dealer. The auction catalogue described it as a copy made in 1327 that was somewhat rubbed and damp-stained, a description that helped keep its true age hidden for generations. Smithsonian Magazine reported that the London dealer Sweet & Maxwell had bought the parchment at Sotheby’s for £42 only about a month before Harvard acquired it.The parchment measures about 489 by 473 millimetres, or roughly 19 inches by 19 inches. It was part of Harvard Law School Library’s collection of historic documents and had even been placed on display. Digital images were also available online, meaning the document was not completely hidden from researchers. Its significance, however, remained unnoticed until a medieval historian happened to examine those images. ABC News reported that library staff had continued to regard it as a cheap copy even while it was on display.What first revealed the document’s true identityDavid Carpenter, a professor of medieval history at King’s College London, was studying digitised Magna Carta material in December 2023 when he came across HLS MS 172 on Harvard’s website. The handwriting, layout and overall appearance immediately suggested to him that the parchment could be an original from 1300 rather than the later copy recorded in the catalogue. He then contacted Nicholas Vincent, a medieval historian at the University of East Anglia, to help investigate.The researchers had several clues to examine. Harvard Law School reported that the document’s dimensions matched those of the 6 previously known originals from 1300. Its handwriting also showed distinctive features, including a large capital E at the beginning of Edwardus and elongated letters in the opening line. Those details were consistent with the other surviving originals.The researchers then faced a more difficult problem. Much of the writing had faded, making a direct comparison challenging. Harvard librarians used ultraviolet light and spectral imaging to reveal details that could not be seen clearly with the naked eye. The scans made it possible to examine the faded writing and compare the document closely with the other known originals from 1300.Why the edition from 1300 was so importantThe Magna Carta had first been issued in 1215 under King John and established a lasting principle that the monarch was subject to the law. The charter later became an important influence on constitutional traditions in Britain and elsewhere, including the development of the United States’ founding documents. ABC News noted that several updated editions followed the original, including the version issued by Edward I in 1300.That 1300 edition is particularly significant because it was the last time the full Magna Carta was set out and authorised by the king’s seal. According to PBS NewsHour, it was the 6th and final version in a sequence of editions issued after the original, while Smithsonian Magazine described Edward I’s 1300 reissue as the last time an English king confirmed the Magna Carta.Before Harvard’s discovery, six original copies from the 1300 issue were known. The identification of HLS MS 172 therefore increased that number to 7. Harvard Law School said the document is now recognised as one of only seven surviving originals from that particular issue.How did scholars confirm the parchment was genuineCarpenter and Vincent did not rely simply on its appearance. They compared the text against the other originals and found that it matched the authorised wording. Harvard Law School reported that the seven documents were examined alongside one another and that the clerks who produced them had been instructed to follow a prepared text closely. Any significant difference could therefore have raised doubts about the Harvard parchment.Instead, the document passed the comparison with extremely strong results. Ultraviolet and spectral images helped reveal writing that had become difficult to see over time, allowing the researchers to compare the wording closely. PBS reported that the scholars also examined the handwriting and the physical dimensions, finding them consistent with the known originals.The discovery also changed the estimated importance of what had been sitting in Harvard’s collection. Carpenter estimated that the parchment could be worth millions of dollars. A 1297 Magna Carta sold for $21.3 million at auction in 2007, although Harvard has no plans to sell its newly authenticated document.Where had Harvard’s Magna Carta come fromAuthenticating the parchment was only part of the mystery. Vincent also investigated its earlier history and traced a possible route back to Appleby in Westmorland, England. Harvard Law School reported that the document was sent to auction in 1945 by First World War flying ace Forster Sammy Maynard.Maynard had inherited archives connected with Thomas and John Clarkson, prominent campaigners against the slave trade. Thomas Clarkson had later retired to the English Lake District and became friendly with William Wordsworth and William Lowther, who was associated with Appleby. Researchers believe the Magna Carta may have passed from Appleby through the Lowthers and Clarksons before reaching Maynard and eventually the auction market.That final part of the story is not completely proven. Vincent said the evidence strongly suggests that Harvard’s parchment could be the lost Magna Carta once issued to Appleby, but further documentation would be needed to establish the connection conclusively.You use AI every day. articles.title: Veteran walked across four continents and just swam the English Channel to return home
articles.summary: British Army veteran Karl Bushby reached England after 28 years and 30,000 miles, but he still has 250 miles to walk to reunite with his mother in the port city of Hull.
articles.body: A British Army veteran has returned to his home country after a 28-year journey across four continents — but his trek isn't quite over. Karl Bushby, a 57-year-old former paratrooper, reached England this week after swimming across the English Channel from France, marking the latest milestone in an around-the-world expedition that he embarked on in 1998. Now, he has roughly 250 miles left to walk before reuniting with his mother, whom he hasn't seen in 11 years. DIVERS BRAVE DEADLY 'MOUNT EVEREST OF SHIPWRECKS' AS FAMED WRECK BREAKS APART Bushby spent about 20 hours swimming in the English Channel over three days before reaching Shakespeare Beach near Dover on Oct. 5, according to the BBC. "Getting in the water that first day, I thought, 'Have I taken too much of a bite here?'" Bushby told the outlet. "But you dig deep. Keep on keeping on. You find a rhythm." Bushby hadn't even trained for the last leg of the trip and after about an hour in the water, he was cramping and doubting whether he could finish, he told the BBC. CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER But the Channel crossing was just the latest obstacle in an expedition spanning more than 30,000 miles and 29 countries. Bushby set out from Chile on Nov. 1, 1998, and set two rules for himself: He would not use transportation including planes, trains, boats or cars to advance his expedition route and he would not return home to Hull until he had finished it. His route took him the length of South America, through North America and across the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Along the way, he trekked through the Darién Gap between Panama and Colombia and, in 2006, crossed the frozen Bering Strait on foot and over ice with Dimitri Kieffer, a French-American adventurer. More recently, Bushby swam about 184 miles across the Caspian Sea before continuing west toward Europe. His expedition faced delays related to visa restrictions, the loss of sponsors during the 2008 financial crisis, COVID-19 lockdowns and geopolitical turmoil, according to reports. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Bushby began his expedition with just $500 and no sponsors, relying over the years on book sales, speaking engagements, donations and corporate sponsorships to keep going. A documentary production company also provided support for the past 16 years, according to reports. When Bushby finally reached France, he was hoping to cross into England on foot through the Channel Tunnel's service tunnel, which connects both countries, but his request was rejected over safety and maintenance concerns, according to the BBC, leaving him to swim the English Channel instead. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Bushby said floating on his back at night and looking at the stars offered a distraction from the physical pain he was in during the swim. "You're far away from light pollution and have the whole night sky in front of you," he said. "It gave me something to think about and took my mind off the pain and aches. It was amazing." The last leg of the journey will bring him to his mother, who he hasn't seen since 2015, in the port city of Hull, The Times of London reported. He is expected to arrive in early November. "That’s about 400 kilometers from here, so I’ve got to get busy."

articles.body: From Mahatma Gandhi's great-grandson being held for 10 hours in Mumbai to police stopping marches in multiple cities, Saturday's anti-SIR protests triggered detentions and security clampdowns across states. Demonstrators demanded CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and withdrawal of SIR of poll rolls.In Mumbai, cops detained Tushar Gandhi, actor Imran Khan and others, while barricades blocked access to August Kranti Maidan. Tushar was picked up near National College at 9.30am and released at 7.30pm. His daughter Kasturi Gandhi was also detained. She said overcrowded police stations forced police to take her farther away. Hundreds gathered near the maidan in small groups, shouting slogans and causing traffic congestion.In Pune, police detained 92 people attempting to hold a rally without permission. They were released after a few hours. In Nashik, 26 protesters, including six women, were detained during a march attended by around 300 people demanding Kumar's removal.In Vijayawada, police stopped a Congress, CPI and CPM-backed march towards Lok Bhavan to submit a memorandum to the governor. Several politicians and activists were detained, while others were placed under house arrest.In Prayagraj, Disha Chhatra Sangathan and Naujawan Bharat Sabha protested against SIR, Kumar and EVMs, demanding cancellation of SIR and a return to ballot-paper voting. Heavy police deployment, drones and cameras outnumbered protesters.In Ranchi, RJD held a procession alleging vote theft and opposing the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act.In Guwahati, 300 people gathered at Chachal in solidarity with CJP-led protests in Delhi. articles.title: Anxiety treatable, but 83% of affected did not get help
articles.summary: Whenever Thane businessman Shekhar travels to south Mumbai for a meeting, he sets off over three hours early.
articles.body: Whenever Thane businessman Shekhar travels to south Mumbai for a meeting, he sets off over three hours early. This is because he plans his route carefully to ensure he is never more than five minutes from a hospital in case he "suffers a heart attack while driving".Karthik (32), an IIM graduate with a high-powered marketing job, dreads routine meetings. "There is this heaviness in my stomach and my legs seem leaden. It's a paralysing fear that stays until the meeting is over," he says.Shekhar and Karthik (names changed) have anxiety disorders, a group of conditions that can turn ordinary journeys, workplace interactions and social situations into emotional ordeals.The invisible burdenNational Mental Health Survey, conducted by National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) across 12 states between 2014 and 2016, found that 2.57% of adults had an anxiety disorder at the time of assessment.Around 83% of those affected were not receiving treatment, while nearly 60% experienced disability of varying severity, according to the study published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 2022."Anxiety disorders are frequently under-recognised and inadequately treated. Stigma surrounding mental illness and a lack of awareness contribute to the problem," said psychiatrist Dr Kedar Tilwe of Fortis Hospital, Mulund.Child psychiatrist Dr Kersi Chavda said anxiety can take many forms, from social anxiety and academic stress to persistent, intrusive thoughts.In children, it may manifest as school refusal. Among adolescents facing examinations, anxiety can also present as headaches, body aches or backaches.Social anxiety is another concern, said Dr Chavda. The pressure to appear perfect, amplified by curated virtual lives on social media, can intensify the fear of being judged or found wanting.When the body's alarm won't switch offEveryday anxiety is a normal response to uncertainty or danger. An anxiety disorder involves persistent or disproportionate fear that interferes with daily life.A senior psychologist from a civic hospital linked anxiety to the body's built-in alarm system. The alarm is meant to respond to a threat, but sometimes it reacts to a gust of wind as though an intruder were approaching.Psychiatrist Dr Harish Shetty said, "Crowded trains, inadequate sleep, workplace demands, educational pressures, financial worries and concerns about personal safety can keep people in a state of heightened stress."Weakening support systems and reduced emotional connectedness may also be contributing, said Dr Shetty.Life in the slow laneIn adults, panic disorder can be accompanied by agoraphobia - fear of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable if a panic attack occurs."Patients may avoid bri-dges, crowded trains, flights or traffic jams. Some will not travel without their spouses or may turn down promotions or jobs that require them to venture beyond familiar surroundi-ngs," said Dr Tilwe. As a result, he added, it's a life lived in second gear: not ready to take up new challenges as one prefers to stick to known schedules.It's treatableAnxiety disorders are treatable, but a trained physician is needed to recognise the problem. Treatment depends on the type and severity of the disorder and may involve psychotherapy, medication or both. "A person with a severe anxiety disorder may need counselling along with medication for up to six months to be able to cope," said Dr Tilwe.Dr Shetty recommends attention to sleep, time management, breathing exercises and meditation. Doctors said reducing excessive caffeine and smoking would help some people manage symptoms.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Myanmar's young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to the army
articles.summary: A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and and civilian resistance.
articles.body:
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.

"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.

"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."

Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.

According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.

Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.

Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.

The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.

Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.

"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.

The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.

They said they had no comment on the matter.

With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.

The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.

International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.

In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.

Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.

"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.

Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.

"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."

Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.

"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."

Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.

The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.

In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.

U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.

When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.

But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.

"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.

"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.

"I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."

In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.

The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.

She does not know where her husband is now.

Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.

Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.

"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."

In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.

The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.

BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.

"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.

"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."

While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.

So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.

Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".

But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.

It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.

The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".

In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.

Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.

As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."

articles.title: New Zealand replaced this 1904 bridge with a modern crossing after 112 years; locals saved the historic structure, now the country’s only surviving steel cantilever road bridge
articles.summary: A 1904 bridge in New Zealand has outlived the road traffic it was built to carry.
articles.body: A 1904 bridge in New Zealand has outlived the road traffic it was built to carry. The Mangaweka Cantilever Bridge spans the Rangitīkei River in the central North Island, where its steel trusses have stood for more than a century. Heritage New Zealand reported that when a routine inspection in 2016 found serious structural deterioration, a new crossing was built nearby and the old bridge was closed to vehicles. Yet it was not demolished. Strong local support helped secure its future, and the historic structure reopened for pedestrians and cyclists. Its survival also preserves a rare engineering design, as it remains New Zealand’s only steel cantilever road bridge.What drove New Zealand to build the Mangaweka bridgeThe bridge emerged from a practical problem that had become increasingly difficult to ignore as settlement expanded through the region. The Mōkai Pātea area had long been home to Māori communities, including Ngāti Hauiti, while Pākehā settlement increased during the 19th century through leases, land purchases and the development of farming and forestry.The North Island Main Trunk railway helped connect the area, while growing numbers of settlers and travellers needed reliable ways to cross the Rangitīkei River. Earlier crossings had served the area, but the river could be difficult and dangerous, particularly in a region prone to flooding.Residents repeatedly called for a safer crossing. The response was the construction of the Mangaweka bridge on the site of earlier river crossings. Its design was shaped by the river itself. Rather than placing supports in the middle of the water, engineers used a cantilever arrangement that allowed the main structure to span the river without a midstream pier. That was an important consideration in a flood-prone location.A rare cantilever design gave the Mangaweka bridge its historic statusAs reported by Heritage New Zealand, the bridge was designed and constructed under the direction of the Public Works Department, with the engineering firm J and A Anderson Ltd also associated with the work. Its form was unusual for New Zealand.The single-lane crossing measures about 141 metres and consists of three steel truss spans with a timber deck. Two concrete piers already stood at the site, having originally been constructed for a cylinder bridge that was never completed. Those structures were extended and incorporated into the eventual cantilever bridge.The result was a type of crossing that was rarely used elsewhere in the country. Heritage records identify Mangaweka as the first and only steel cantilever road bridge constructed in New Zealand. It is also one of only three known surviving cantilever bridges in the country.Mangaweka bridge became part of New Zealand’s farming and forestry historyThe bridge occupies a striking position within the surrounding landscape. Rather than sitting high above the river, it runs lower between the surrounding hills, giving people crossing it a different view of the valley and river environment. For generations, that setting was experienced from behind the wheel or from a vehicle travelling across the single-lane deck. Today, the crossing can be appreciated at a slower pace.Its connection to the surrounding countryside is also part of its heritage value. The bridge helped support the settlement and development of farming and forestry across the central Manawatū-Whanganui region, making it part of a much wider story than its steelwork alone suggests.A century passed before its official openingThere is an unusual detail in the bridge's history. Although plans were made for an official opening around the time construction was completed, the ceremony did not actually take place until 111 years later.By then, the bridge had already spent most of its life carrying people and vehicles across the river. It had also undergone repairs over the decades, but its basic form remained largely intact.The longevity of the structure is reflected in how little its original design changed. The steel trusses, timber deck and overall arrangement retained the character of the crossing built at the beginning of the 20th century.For a working road bridge, that continuity was remarkable. But eventually the demands placed on it became greater than its structure could accommodate.A new bridge changed its futureIn 2016, a routine inspection found significant structural deterioration. The old crossing was no longer considered capable of meeting modern traffic requirements, effectively bringing its use as a road bridge to an end.A replacement was constructed about 30 metres to the south. From a transport perspective, the decision provided a modern crossing better suited to contemporary traffic. The older bridge faced a very different question: whether it should remain at all.Demolition had been considered, but there was strong local support for keeping the historic structure. The community response reflected more than nostalgia for an old road. The bridge was tied to the development of the surrounding settlements, the history of transport through the district and the distinctive landscape around the Rangitīkei River.Mangaweka bridge remains in use after traffic moves to a modern crossingInstead of being removed, Mangaweka Cantilever Bridge reopened as a pedestrian and cycling crossing. Its role changed, but the structure itself remained. That has allowed the bridge to continue serving the area without having to carry modern road traffic. It is now part of the recreational and tourism experience around Mangaweka, offering visitors a way to cross the river while seeing the historic steelwork at close range.There is also something practical about the arrangement. The new bridge handles the demands of modern vehicles, while the older one remains available for slower forms of travel. The two structures occupy different roles rather than competing for the same purpose. For the historic bridge, that distinction has made continued survival possible.You use AI every day. articles.title: WHO says no plague case registered after Russian lab worker’s death
articles.summary: The WHO says the lack of a confirmed diagnosis remains a key uncertainty, with no sign of ongoing transmission.
articles.body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has said it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a laboratory worker at a Russian plague research institute and that no case of plague has been registered.

Russia’s state health regulator told the WHO that tests on the worker and people who had been in contact with her were negative for the dangerous pathogens they tested for, the United Nations health agency said in a statement on Saturday.

Her contacts still showed no symptoms, and no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been found, the WHO added.

“Based on the information provided… WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker,” it said.

The worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and stoking public health fears on social media.

Russian media named her as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, in the Siberian region of Irkutsk.

Pneumonic plague, a lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas, was suspected early on.

The governor of neighbouring Buryatia said the woman had “died, maybe of the plague”.

Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said she had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.

Russian authorities said the worker was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body. They say post-mortem tests did not detect plague.

On Thursday, Russia said it had completed health checks on all her contacts and had given the WHO all the information.

A local official said on October 6 that 60 percent of those placed in quarantine had already been released.

WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus asked Russia on Wednesday to respond to media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. Russia dismissed the reports as “false information”.

The United States has also called on Russia for transparency.

Global health officials have been extra alert to deadly pneumonia cases of unknown cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading, fatal respiratory illness in China.

The cause of individual pneumonia cases often cannot be determined.

articles.title: AI is creating a 'human premium' for art created by people
articles.summary: Amid a surge in AI content, many are placing extra value on art that's obviously made by a human. But can that last, asks Ros Atkins
articles.body:
A few weeks back, in a former bank building that's now a music venue in Falmouth, Cornwall, I was DJ-ing at a night I run called Rave Machine. It was a noisy, high-energy, sweaty affair, just as a night's dancing should be.

All of the elements - the crowd, performers, staff, music, the journey home - connected to create something special, a one-off. It was also completely human.

Something, in theory, well out of reach of what technology could possibly offer.

In the DJ world, though, technology has already changed the equation. In the 1990s, a DJ had to not only pick the tracks, but also thread them together armed only with vinyl records, a pair of turntables and a mixer. Now, much more assistance is on offer, including software that will sync beats on different tracks should you ask it to (I don't). Apple Music and Spotify have an AI tune-mixing option too.

If you were out dancing, would it matter to you if a DJ was, well, not really DJing? If you loved the music being played, would you care if technology was doing the work?

It's a question that generative AI - the type of AI that creates content - is asking of us all. One of the thrills of that night in Falmouth was seeing our special guest, Andy Cato from Groove Armada, artfully weaving an array of tracks. How would I feel if a DJ was just pressing play? (And that does happen).

I mention all of this because that experience in Falmouth connects to a far broader question: whether we actually care if a piece of art has been created by a human, be that a painting, song, book, poem, or any other type of art.

Renaissance frescoes and chess champions

The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated. Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't. But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI. They want humans to be involved.

Daniel Susskind, an economics professor at King's College London, says many of us place huge value on the human role in making art. It's what makes the creative process different from more functional, practical tasks, he thinks.

"I was once in a room of accountants, and one of them stood up and said, 'My clients come to me for the personal touch, the human process'," he remembers. "And I said, 'That isn't why they come to you, they come because they want their taxes done properly'."

But it's different with art, he says. "If I walk into the Sistine Chapel and look at the ceiling, I think not only is that extraordinarily beautiful, but isn't it amazing that a human hand, flesh and blood like my own, came up with that. A mind like mine dreamt that up," he says.

As Susskind describes it, what we value isn't just the destination, it's the knowledge that a human - one of us - got us there. We can wonder at that achievement.

Of course, it could be argued that computers and AI software were themselves created by humans. If Susskind feels awe walking into the Sistine Chapel, others might experience awe of a different type using a chatbot like ChatGPT.

Susskind points to another example, this time a chess match in 1997, when a world champion, Garry Kasparov, lost for the first time to a computer, Deep Blue. At the time, there were fears the computer's success would mean our interest in chess would wane. In fact, chess is more popular than ever, played by millions.

"It wasn't simply the moves on the board that people care about. It's the fact that it's a human being sitting behind them, moving those pieces along that matters," Susskind argues.

And some think that the advent of AI has actually placed extra value on things created by people. You might call that a human premium.

Kyle Chayka, a journalist at The New Yorker focused on technology, says AI writing is now widely considered to be "generic, obsequious and banal". As a result, he says, "I think readers are coming to value very obviously personal writing, and maybe even writing that's messier, less structurally sound or composed or perfected, than they maybe once would've desired."

Chayka goes on: "I think illustration and graphic design is going in the same direction, where the average is too easily accessible, and so designers are leaning into being weirder and more eye-catching and more unusual, trying to find things that AI can't generate so easily."

In response to the surge in AI-created content, academics are racing to develop a universally recognised symbol to denote something that is "human made" (similar to the "Fairtrade" label that emerged in the 1980s). Labels like "AI-free" are already appearing on covers of some books, films, and albums.

For C Thi Nguyen, a philosophy professor at the University of Utah, it's a question of our underlying values.

He says you can often work out your values by following what he calls a "why chain". If you like something or want to do something, ask "why?". If the answer is to make money or be successful, keep asking 'why?' When the process ends, that will be what you really value, he explains.

The question, he says, is whether human involvement and shared human experience will keep its place at the end of the "why chain".

Author John Lanchester is optimistic. He thinks the value of what only humans can do will prevail. In fact, he sympathises with the idea of a 'human premium'.

"If you commodify one kind of thing, the things you can't commodify start to seem more important," he tells me.

All of that might sound heartening for people hoping that humans will remain central to the creation of culture.

But I'm not so sure. The amount of AI-generated content is increasing so quickly that we may soon struggle to distinguish what has or hasn't involved AI.

You may well have seen coverage of the AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood, made last year by a company that bills itself as the world's "first AI talent studio". The Screen Actors Guild in the US was not impressed. "It has no life experience to draw from, no emotion, and, from what we've seen, audiences aren't interested in watching computer-generated content untethered from the human experience," they wrote.

I'm not saying AI will replace actors - of course not. But what feels untethered and strange now, may not, in some situations, feel so strange in time.

It's also worth remembering that long before Large Language Models went mainstream, we'd already allowed technology to shape our cultural tastes.

As recently as the 2000s, we still sought out lots of the culture we consumed. We'd buy a book, a cinema ticket, an album. Sometimes we still do.

But increasingly, culture just arrives - in an endless stream, sorted and served by an algorithm that is constantly predicting our tastes.

At first glance, this sounds convenient. The work's being done for us. But as the role of the algorithm goes up, so the role of humans goes down.

"There's the mythical figure of your big brother's friend or something, who passes on good music taste to you," says Chayka, whose book Filterworld explores the impacts of algorithms on culture. "And now we rely on algorithmic recommendations to do that same thing for us. To introduce us to new things."

I recognise this from my own habits. Back in the 1990s, when I started collecting dance music, I'd find new music through record shops and recommendations from people I trusted. I can still do that, and do. But these days the algorithm's doing a lot of that work for me - and it can be really helpful. I'll find tunes I wouldn't have discovered otherwise.

To an extent, I am letting technology guide me.

Chayka thinks algorithms have made us lazy, and "prevent us from going deeper" in our cultural taste. Sometimes we might find a piece of art that requires work - a long, difficult book, perhaps, or a weird-seeming movie. "It might alienate us initially, but eventually it inspires us," Chayka says.

"I think that kind of culture has fallen by the wayside in favour of culture as content to consume that's not going to change your life, it's just going to turn your brain off for a few hours."

And it's a self-reinforcing loop; creators adapt their work as they seek out the attention the algorithm can provide.

And here's the key point: this shift - to discovering culture via algorithms - is one we've already largely accepted. So when AI starts making books, films, and music in large numbers - might we just shrug and accept that too?

Back in 1986, in Washington DC, protesting teachers lined the streets outside a convention centre. They weren't angry about their wages or budget cuts. In this case, the object of their ire was the calculator. Maths teacher John Saxon had taken up the cause. "The kids are not learning their math facts because they're becoming calculator hooked," he proclaimed. " If they had given me a black box, I wouldn't know that… six times eight's 48 'cause it rhymes, and seven times nine is 63 'cause it does not."

We all have our ways of remembering times tables.

Needless to say, this is an argument that Saxon lost. But some of those arguments feel familiar.

Of course, some things are definitely out of range of technology, at least for now. Think of my sweaty DJ night in Falmouth a few weeks ago, with 250 other ravers.

Alex Mahon says she's noticed an uptick in appreciation for in-person experiences like these - perhaps as a backlash to the amount of our lives now spent on a smartphone screen.

She's chief executive of Superstruct Entertainment, one of the world's leading festival and live entertainment groups.

Tech billionaires seem to be doom prepping. Should we all be worried?

China is winning one AI race, the US another - but either might pull ahead

AI 'slop' is transforming social media - and a backlash is brewing

"People want to go to more live things," she says. "They want to have things that are unforeseeable… unpredictable. The special moment is live. The excitement, the discovery is hearing it in person with others."

In the case of culture, when is it OK to outsource to technology, and when is it not? The more I look at this, the less I'm sure we can assume what choices we'll make.

Each of us will have to decide when it matters if something is made by a human.
